name: create_working_copy
description:
Make a working copy for this project and staff it.

One call. The harness makes the checkout on its own disk and writes the
identity into it; the server records the copy and starts the agents that will
work in it. An agent asking for somewhere to work does not sequence a disk
operation against a database write — the moment it does, every caller has to
get the ordering and the failure handling right, and they each get it wrong
differently.

Story 891 grew this scope on 2026-09-04. Its question `2ec33878` had asked
whether onboarding creates the worktree or runs inside one that already
exists, and answered the second way — so making the copy belonged to nobody.
Story 956's title says "a minted working copy" and none of its thirteen
criteria mint anything; 964 hands an epic to a copy and assumes one. A
project's first epic therefore had nowhere to go but the main checkout, where
a roster is refused because the main copy holds one agent and it is the
project's own.

## Refused rather than half-made

A project with no harness connected has no machine to make a checkout on, and
the answer is a refusal. Writing the row anyway would leave something every
consumer downstream believes in — the failure `EpicDispatch` had to grow a
guard against, where the page said "Being built on your project's checkout"
about a directory that does not exist.

That is the opposite of what `EpicDispatch.approve/2` does with an epic that
has nowhere to go, and deliberately: agreeing to build something is a decision
that survives having nowhere to build it. Asking for a checkout is a request
for a thing.

label.description: What this copy is for, e.g. the epic it will build. Names the directory.

roles.description: Who to staff it with, comma-separated: main, product, coding, qa. Defaults to product,coding,qa — the three that build something. Name your own when you need a particular shape, e.g. `main` alone.

root.description: Where to put it. Defaults to a worktree beside the project's checkout; pass one only when it has to go somewhere specific.

name: ensure_app_running
description:
Bring up the caller's own copy of the app, starting it if it isn't already
running. A live process is health-checked, not automatically restarted when
HEAD moves. If it is unhealthy, the error reports the current checkout HEAD,
the last recorded app revision, and the app log to inspect before recovery.
A healthy app whose served revision differs from HEAD, or whose revision
cannot be verified, returns an error refusing QA against it. The process
stays running; restart_app refreshes it explicitly.

Story 1108's rule: an agent on a copy can start, restart and stop its own
copy's app. Always the caller's own copy -- resolved from the connection's
scope, never a parameter a caller could point at a different one. That is
what makes "an agent cannot reach another copy's app" structural rather
than a check that could be bypassed: there is nothing on this schema to
name another copy with.

## Returns when the run starts, not when it finishes

A first boot compiles, which can run well past the code-mode sandbox's
30s wall clock (issue f2977826, batch 2 of 4f7929e4) -- this used to
shrink its own wait to fit that budget instead, racing it with a margin.
The spawned task claims this working copy's own lock -- shared with
`restart_app` and `stop_app`, since all three touch the same app process
-- and only then acks: the reply is "started" or "already running"; an
agent that started it is messaged the outcome, any other caller calls
this tool again to check.

name: list_working_copies
description:
The checkouts this project has, and what is running on each.

So that deciding where an epic goes can be a decision. John: *"if there's an
appropriate working copy and agent then it should get assigned that, or maybe
the agent wants a fresh working copy ... the user should be able to decide
where to assign it or the agent should be able to decide."*

Neither could, before this: there was no agent-facing way to see a project's
checkouts at all, so "an appropriate one" was not a judgement anything could
make.

## What to look at

`root` is the only thing that makes a row a checkout — a row with none has no
disk behind it and nothing can be built there. `agents` is what is already
running, which is the difference between assigning to a copy that can pick the
work up and assigning to an idle one that needs an agent started first.

`main` is the project's own checkout, the one story 963's agent runs in. It is
a fine destination and not automatically the right one; a copy already holding
a related epic often is.

name: offboard_working_copy
description:
Discard a working copy, ending the agents on it.

The other end of `create_working_copy`. Story 964's rule: *a working copy is
the boundary of the work, and discarding it ends its agents and its
conversation*. John, 2026-09-04: *"I can keep them through that whole epic and
then I can discard the working copy and then come up with another one — that's
how I need to control these boundaries."*

A boundary is only usable if both ends are reachable by whoever is doing the
work. Until this existed, `offboard` was a control on the working-copies page
and nothing else, so an agent could be given a copy and never let go of one.

## What it does not do

Remove the directory. The copy stops being this project's and its agents stop
running; the checkout on disk is left for a person. Deleting a worktree
somebody may have put uncommitted work in is not a thing to do on an agent's
say-so, and the row going is what makes everything downstream stop pointing at
it.

## An agent that would not stop is reported, not swallowed

The copy this is most often used on is one whose machine has gone — that is
story 892's premise — so failing to reach an agent cannot block the offboard.
It is said instead: the process may still be running, and ending it is the
operator's, because the server could not reach it to try.

working_copy_id.description: Id of the working copy to discard. `list_working_copies` names them.

name: restart_app
description:
Restart the caller's own copy of the app, on its current commit.

See `EnsureAppRunning` -- same "always the caller's own copy, never a
parameter" reasoning applies here.

## Returns when the run starts, not when it finishes

A restart waits for a recompile and a boot, which can run well past the
code-mode sandbox's 30s wall clock (issue f2977826, batch 2 of 4f7929e4)
-- this used to shrink its own wait to fit that budget instead, racing it
with a margin. The spawned task claims this working copy's own lock --
shared with `stop_app` and `ensure_app_running`, since all three touch
the same app process, and a restart racing another restart's own
`_build` directory is exactly the hazard this closes -- and only then
acks: the reply is "started" or "already running". A second restart_app
call while one is in flight never starts a second one; it is told the
one already running is still going. An agent that started it is messaged
the outcome; any other caller calls this tool again to check.

name: set_working_copy_loop
description:
Put a working copy's agents to work, or let them stop.

Story 538's R13. Continuous mode governs whether an agent keeps working when
its turn ends, and until this it had no front door: the only way in was an
agent happening to work the `start_implementation` task, and the only way out
was `tap_out`, which asks a human. Every agent in the database sat at `false`
because nothing had ever put one anywhere else.

## What "working" means here

Not that anything is assigned. The loop hands back the menu — a class of
available work and the tool call that opens it — and the agent chooses. John,
2026-09-05: *"I'm dubious our orchestrator will make better decisions than the
model with the upcoming requirements and some reasoning."* So this switches on
the thing that keeps an agent going, not a thing that tells it what to do.

## Per copy, because that is the unit somebody decides about

A checkout is working or it is not. The roles staffed on it each carry their
own mode, so a later change can let the coding agent go home when coding work
runs out while QA carries on (R6) — but nobody wants to switch agents on one
at a time.

## Stopping is not killing

Turning it off lets the agents stop at the end of their current turn. It does
not end them: they stay on the copy, keep their conversations, and can be put
back to work. `offboard_working_copy` is the one that ends things.

working.description: true puts its agents in the loop — each keeps working, choosing from the menu, until nothing of its kind is left. false lets them stop after the turn they are on.

working_copy_id.description: Id of the working copy. `list_working_copies` names them.

name: share_copy_app
description:
Give the caller's own copy a public preview address.

Shares its device's tunnel rather than provisioning one of its own —
criteria 1586/1587: a same-device sibling's connector can already reach
this copy's local port, so its hostname is added to that tunnel's ingress
instead of standing up a second connector nothing needs.

Always the caller's own copy, never a parameter — same "an agent cannot
reach another copy" reasoning as `EnsureAppRunning`/`StopApp`. Refused
while the copy's own app is not serving: sharing points a public hostname
at a local port, and a port nothing is listening on yet is exactly the gap
between "reported" and "actually up" story 1108's `app_url` exists to
close.

name: stop_app
description:
Stop the caller's own copy of the app.

See `EnsureAppRunning` -- same "always the caller's own copy, never a
parameter" reasoning applies here. A copy with nothing running answers
success too, same as `AppTransport.stop_app/2` itself.

## Returns when the run starts, not when it finishes

Stopping is normally fast, but this used to hold the code-mode sandbox's
entire 30s budget inline with no margin to even return an answer
afterward (issue f2977826, batch 2 of 4f7929e4). The spawned task claims
this working copy's own lock -- shared with `restart_app` and
`ensure_app_running`, since all three touch the same app process -- and
only then acks: the reply is "started" or "already running"; an agent
that started it is messaged the outcome, any other caller calls this
tool again to check.

name: sync_working_copy
description:
Bring a working copy's checkout up to date with its remote's main.

8f5ebfb2: asked to staff a working copy reported days behind main, there
was no reachable way to catch it up first -- `list_working_copies`,
`create_working_copy`, `offboard_working_copy`, `set_working_copy_loop` and
`assign_epic_to_working_copy` all leave the checkout on disk untouched, and
`sync_project` reconciles the CALLING copy's own files against its
database row rather than fetching or merging anything. This reaches the
named copy's own harness over the same channel `offboard_working_copy`
already addresses it through.

Fast-forward only, and refused on a dirty tree -- never a merge commit or a
merge into someone's uncommitted work made on this call's own say-so. Both
failure shapes are reported with the git output that explains them, so the
decision of what to do next stays with whoever is staffing the copy.

working_copy_id.description: Id of the working copy to sync. `list_working_copies` names them.

name: unshare_copy_app
description:
Drop the caller's own copy's shared preview.

Removes the ingress rule that pointed its hostname at this copy's app and
the DNS record behind it, and clears the copy's own recorded address. See
`ShareCopyApp`.

A no-op on main, whose tunnel is the project's rather than this call's to
remove, and on a copy that was never shared — see `PreviewTunnel.release/1`.
